name: Tokyo
description: Marunouchi and Ginza to Tokyo Tower: red-brick Tokyo Station, the Imperial Palace moats, Ginza's grand boulevard, Hibiya Park, the water bus on the bay and the orange-and-white tower at sunset.

bridges.note: Central Tokyo's bridges over the rivers and the Imperial Palace's moats; forms from each bridge's record (Tokyo Metropolitan Government, Chiyoda and Chuo wards).

勝鬨橋.note: 1940, the bascule between two tied arches

築地大橋.note: 2018, a three-span half-through steel arch, white

日本橋.note: 1911, a granite double arch (Tsumaki Yorinaka; bronzes by Watanabe Osao): the two lamp standards over the pier with their kirin back to back, the four end pillars with their lamps and the lions holding the city's crest (Chuo City; photographs)

常盤橋.note: 1926, a two-span arch faced in stone

和田倉橋.note: 1953, concrete under a wooden-style railing with bronze giboshi

皇居正門石橋.note: 1887, the granite double arch (Meganebashi), bronze candelabra

皇居正門鉄橋 「二重橋」.note: 1964 steel, to the 1888 iron bridge's design, black; a level deck between the moat's walls at the Seimon terrace's height (16.7 m, GSI's laser over the flat terrace at its south end; the palace side is 16.5 to 17 m), the walls standing to it (cities/tokyo/moats.py WALLED)

seawall.note: The rivers' and the bay's revetments and the castle moats: granite blocks and concrete.

susuki.note: Susuki (trees.json susuki, #326): on the open grassland and meadows OpenStreetMap maps (natural=grassland, landuse=meadow: the unmown grass of the parks and the hills, where susuki is the grass that stands) (Overture base land, OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL; pipeline/grasses.py). Its heads stand from mid August to spring (web/trees.js).

trees.note: Species are not mapped; the mix is a guess from the cities' street-tree surveys and the parks' own guides: ginkgo and zelkova (keyaki) are Japan's commonest street trees, with plane trees and camphor; the woods are the laurel forest's evergreen broadleaves and camphors, with zelkovas, black pines, maples and a few cedars (sugi, standing for hinoki too). Areas give the parks and precincts known for their own trees a mix of their own; their outlines are OpenStreetMap's (pipeline/tree_areas.py). Somei-yoshino cherries (sakura) line Tokyo's streets after the ginkgo and the zelkova, and stand in the parks' lawns and along the rivers and moats; areas give the places known for them a mix of their own.

areas.name: Chidorigafuchi
areas.note: Chidorigafuchi Park: the cherries leaning out over the moat by the boat pier (photographs). Lit after dark in the bloom (the Chiyoda Sakura Festival's light-up).

areas.name: Chidorigafuchi Ryokudo
areas.note: The 700 m footpath along the moat under some 260 cherries (Chiyoda City).

areas.name: Kokyo Gaien
areas.note: About two thousand black pines on the outer garden's lawns (the Ministry of the Environment's guide).

areas.name: Kokyo Higashi Gyoen
areas.note: The East Gardens' woods and lawns; by the Ninomaru garden a grove of the prefectures' cherries, from the February kawazu-zakura to the late double ones.

areas.name: Kokyo
areas.note: The palace's own woods (Fukiage): mostly the laurel forest's evergreen broadleaves.

protection.title: No sun-access rule: a lunch-hour test
protection.summary: Tokyo has no rule that protects sun on parks and plazas. The windows here are a thought experiment for this project: what would a new tower cost the lunch hour?
protection.source_note: Windows are our own choice (noon to 13:00, all year), not law. Tokyo's shadow rule, 日影規制 (Building Standards Act, art. 56-2), limits hours of shadow on neighbouring land in designated residential-type zones; it does not cover public places and does not apply in commercial districts such as Marunouchi. Check the ward's zoning before relying on this.
protection.reading_note: Tokyo keeps standard time all year (no daylight saving), so the clock and the sun agree all year. Baseline: the test compares against today's PLATEAU model, which is surveyed to 2020-ish, so towers built since are missing from 76% of the footprint area's heights unless Overture or OSM has them.
protection.tip: Tip: try the block south-west of Hibiya Park, or between the Marunouchi towers and the Palace.

tour.title: Marunouchi to Tokyo Tower
tour.text: Tokyo's front door: the station where every shinkansen line begins, the palace where the emperor lives, Ginza's department stores, and Tokyo Tower glowing orange at the end of the road.

tour.title: Tokyo Station
tour.text: The red-brick Marunouchi building of 1914, restored to its domes in 2012. It sold the air above it to the towers around, so it stays low while Marunouchi grows tall. Buy an ekiben and catch a bullet train.

tour.title: Hibiya Park at lunch
tour.text: Japan's first Western-style park, where office workers bring their bento. On a midwinter noon {sun:Hibiya Park 日比谷公園|12-22|12:00}% of it is in the sun, and by 13:00 {sun:Hibiya Park 日比谷公園|12-22|13:00}%.

tour.title: The National Diet Building
tour.text: Japan's parliament, finished in 1936 after seventeen years of building, in granite and marble quarried across Japan. Its stepped pyramid rises 65 m over Nagatacho, the heart of Japanese politics.

tour.title: Tokyo Tower at sunset
tour.text: 333 m of International Orange and white, opened in 1958 as the symbol of a city rebuilt. Look for its light-up after dark: Landmark Light in warm gold, or Diamond Veil on special nights.

tour.title: After dark
tour.text: The city lights up window by window, from Ginza's neon to the tower's glow. Drag to explore, or open Sun access to test a tower of your own.

rail_osm.note: The JR lines from Tokyo Station to Hamamatsucho, track by track, with their platforms (pipeline/rail_osm.py -> cities/tokyo/rail_osm.json; cities/tokyo/rail.py builds the viaduct, Yurakucho Station and the trains' courses from it).

sources.landmarks: Tokyo Tower: parametric from published dimensions (333 m; decks at 150 m and 250 m; 80 m base), anchored at its published coordinates

weather.source: Tokyo (Kitanomaru Park): Japan Meteorological Agency, 1991-2020 normals, days with at least 0.5 mm

game.title: Tokyo Pilgrimage: Marunouchi & Ginza 東京巡礼・丸の内・銀座
game.blurb: Walk Tokyo from the station to the bay under the real sun. Talk to the people who know it, ride the water bus, and fly to Tokyo Tower.

ferry_style.note: The shared harbour ferry stands in for the water buses and the bay boats; the white and navy are approximate.

game.ferry_note: Piers are from OpenStreetMap via Overture. Routes are generated through open water; the stops follow the real water-bus piers, but the timetable is not real, and the vessel names are those of Tokyo Cruise boats. Boats run at 1.5 times their real speed and wait 20 s at each pier. At a pier you can skip the wait.

scrambles.name: 数寄屋橋 Sukiyabashi
scrambles.note: Harumi-dori and Sotobori-dori in Ginza; scramble-style (jafmate.jp road trivia, 2023-12-25, which names the scramble-style crossings); both diagonals mapped in OSM.

npcs.name: Haruka 遥
idle: 指差呼称 (shisa kanko): we point at every signal and say it aloud, even when no train is coming. Fewer mistakes, they say, by a lot.
Trains here run to the second. If one is 20 seconds late, we apologise. {time} now.

npcs.name: Kenji 健二
idle: Until 1963 Tokyo capped buildings at 31 m, a hundred shaku. Then floor-area ratios replaced the cap.
I eat at my desk or in Hibiya Park, if the sun's out. {sun_line}

npcs.name: Daichi 大地
npcs.role: Palace runner 皇居ランナー
idle: Five kilometres round the Palace, always counter-clockwise. 反時計回り. Nobody told me; everybody does it.
Evening is busiest. By 18:00 you queue at the lockers.

npcs.name: Sachiko 幸子
idle: Hibiya Park opened in 1903, Japan's first Western-style park. My grandmother walked in it in a kimono.
The pigeons know my bag. {sun_line}

npcs.name: Yui 結衣
idle: Ginza at lunch: the main street closes to cars on weekend afternoons. 歩行者天国, the pedestrian paradise.
Lunch is 12:00 to 13:00. Everyone in Marunouchi comes out at once.

npcs.name: Ishikawa-san 石川
idle: いらっしゃいませ! Under the tracks since 1985. The trains overhead? That's the seasoning.
Brick arches from 1910, and every arch is somebody's bar.

npcs.name: Captain Aoki 青木船長
idle: Edo's shogun hunted ducks at Hamarikyu. Now the ducks watch Shiodome's towers.
The Sumida River ends here, and the bay begins. {sun_line}

npcs.name: Hayashi 林
idle: The cabin's warm. Keep clear of the Tokyo Tower lattice: 333 m of steel, and it does not move.

npcs.name: Ren 蓮
idle: Tokyo Tower opened in 1958, at 333 m, 13 m taller than the Eiffel Tower. That was the point.
The orange-and-white paint is for aircraft. It repaints every five years.

npcs.name: Mei 芽依
idle: Navy blazer, a ribbon, and a long walk to school. I love the autumn light on the moat.
My cram school is in Otemachi. It's {time}. {sun_line}

npcs.name: Sato 佐藤
idle: 有楽町、有楽町です。Tracks 2 and 3 are the Yamanote Line, 1 and 4 the Keihin-Tohoku. By day its rapid trains run straight through: stand behind the yellow blocks.
The platforms have stood on these brick arches since 1910. Past track 4 run the Tokaido Line and the Shinkansen: no platform for them here, so they never slow down.
A Shinkansen out of Tokyo Station is sixteen cars, 400 metres. It takes about fifteen seconds to pass us, and it is still only warming up.

npcs.name: Tetsuko 鉄子
idle: The end of platform 4 is the spot: the Yamanote's green E235, the blue Keihin-Tohoku, the orange and green Tokaido, and the white Shinkansen, all in one frame.
Come back at dusk. The cars' windows light up before the sky goes dark, and the towers behind them start to glitter.

npcs.name: Mori 森
idle: Two minutes between trains on the Yamanote. Miss one and the next is already at Shimbashi.
Listen for the melody: when it stops, the doors close. Every station has its own.

lines.title: Report back
lines.on_open: All three walks done. Report back to Haruka at Tokyo Station.

quests.title: Welcome to Tokyo Station
talk: ようこそ。Welcome to Tokyo Station. I'm Haruka; I work the Marunouchi gates. Red brick, 1914, and in 2012 they gave it back the domes it lost in the war.

Three walks, any order. Marunouchi and the Palace: Kenji, on Naka-dori, knows why the towers are tall and the station low. Ginza: Yui, under the clock at 4-chome. The water and the air: Ishikawa-san, at his grill under the Yurakucho tracks.

The helicopter is on the plaza's north side, taxis wait in the rotary (a hand up at the kerb, Y), and the water buses leave from Hamarikyu, a taxi ride south. WASD to walk, Shift to run, E to talk, T to switch walks. Which first?

choices.text: Marunouchi and the Palace: Kenji, on Naka-dori
Ginza: Yui, under the clock at 4-chome
The water and the air: Ishikawa-san, under the tracks

quests.title: The air above the station
talk: Look at the station: a few storeys of brick. Look at the towers: 200 m of glass. Why does Marunouchi look like that?
Because the station owner sold its unused floor area, its 空中権 (air rights), to the towers nearby. The brick stays low and the money restored it.
Stand on the plaza in front of the station and look back: brick below, glass above. Then go and find Daichi on the Palace plaza. He runs there every day.

steps.text: Stand on the plaza in front of the station
Find Daichi on the Palace plaza

quests.title: Round the Palace
talk: Cooling down. This gravel plaza is the Kokyo Gaien; the moat is Edo Castle's. Edo became Tokyo in 1868.
Yui says lunch is the best hour in Hibiya Park, if the sun's out. Winter, though. In December the sun sits low, and the towers matter. Ask Sachiko.

quests.title: A bench in the sun
talk: Winter lunch in Hibiya Park: that's my favourite hour. On 22 December at noon, {sun:Hibiya Park 日比谷公園|12-22|12:00}% of the park is in direct sun. On 21 June it's {sun:Hibiya Park 日比谷公園|6-21|12:00}%.
No rule protects it, you know. A new tower could take it away. Find a sunny spot for me at lunchtime on the winter solstice. The sun meter under the map tells you when you're in it.

steps.text: Stand in direct sun in Hibiya Park, 12:00 to 13:00 on 22 December

quests.title: Lunch in Ginza
talk: Counting rooflines? Good, somebody should. Ginza's main street keeps them at 56 m: the Ginza Rules, 銀座ルール. The clock over my shoulder has kept the corner's time since 1932.
Skip the department store, though. Ishikawa-san grills under the tracks at Yurakucho, and his yakitori is the real lunch.

steps.text: Find Ishikawa-san under the Yurakucho tracks

quests.title: Under the arches
talk: Yui sent you? Then eat first. These arches are red brick from 1910, and the trains have run over our heads ever since. Every arch between here and Shimbashi is somebody's counter.
Follow the arches north, two minutes. The glass hall shaped like a ship is the Forum: 1997, sixty metres of glass, on the ground where Tokyo's city hall stood until it moved to Shinjuku in 1991.
Walk in under the glass and look up. Then come back hungry.

steps.text: Walk north along the arches to the Tokyo International Forum

quests.title: Water bus
talk: いらっしゃい! Eat. Tokyo is a city of water: the Palace moat, the canals, and the bay out there. Most people forget.

Walk down to Hamarikyu, the shogun's garden. The water bus leaves from the pier there. Ride it to Hinode Pier, then come back round by Harumi and find Captain Aoki on the Hamarikyu landing. Tell him I sent you.

steps.text: Take the water bus from Hamarikyu to Hinode Pier
Find Captain Aoki back on the Hamarikyu landing

quests.title: Tokyo Tower from the air
talk: From the water the city is a wall. Go up. Hayashi's helicopter is on the pad in Hibiya Park.

Fly south-west to Tokyo Tower and land in Shiba Park below it. Space to climb, C to descend, W and S for forward and back, A and D to turn. V is the bird's-eye view. E gets you out once you've landed.

steps.text: Meet Hayashi at the Hibiya Park helipad
Land in Shiba Park, below Tokyo Tower
Find Ren at the foot of Tokyo Tower

quests.title: 333 metres
talk: You flew in? Then you've seen it: {landmark:tokyo_tower.height} m, and the main deck at {landmark:tokyo_tower.main_deck} m. Six hundred steps up, if you'd rather walk.
On a clear winter morning you can see Mt Fuji from the top deck.
That's the water and the air, both. When your other walks are done, Haruka will want to hear about it at the station.

quests.title: The whole loop
talk: お疲れ様でした。That's all three walks: the station and the air above it, the Palace and the sun, Ginza and the arches, the water and the tower.
The city is yours. Change the time of day, take the water bus, or fly anywhere. Come back to the station after dark: the brick is lit.
